tagline.text: A protected bay off Mati and a day trip around three islands

location.label: Location
location.text: Tamisan area, Mati City, Davao Oriental

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Calmest from March to early May

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (per person, sharing a boat; includes island fee and transport)

children.text: Pujada Bay is a protected seascape of about 21,200 hectares in front of Mati City. The classic outing is a full-day island-hopping trip by boat from the Tamisan pier to Pujada, Oak and Waniban islands.

Pujada Bay is a large bay on the Pacific coast of eastern Mindanao, with Mati, the capital of Davao Oriental, at its head. The Guanguan Peninsula and the Pujada Peninsula cradle it like two arms, filtering out the big ocean swells, so the water is far calmer than at neighboring Dahican Beach. On July 31, 1994, President Ramos's Proclamation No. 431 made it the Pujada Bay Protected Landscape and Seascape, covering the bay, its coast and four islands, about
21,200 hectares
in all.

Pujada Island sits at the mouth of the bay and splits the entrance into two channels. The island is covered with trees and shrubs, and a small lighthouse stands at its southeastern tip. Nearby are the tiny sandbar islets of Oak and Ivy, and to the east lies Waniban Island (also spelled Uanivan). When travelers talk about the "Mati island tour," they usually mean a boat trip around Pujada, Oak and Waniban.

The bay is reported to hold more than 25 genera of hard and soft corals, with Montipora, Acropora and Porites the most common. It has about 850 hectares of mangroves, and nine of the Philippines' 16 seagrass species are found here. Because the area is lightly developed, it is quiet, and there are no convenience stores or large restaurants on the islands. You have to bring your own food and drinks, but that is part of the charm. Near Pujada Island you can see where the water changes from the pale turquoise of the inner bay to the deep blue of the open sea, so the boat ride itself is a sight worth savoring.
It takes 3–4 hours by road from Davao City, so most visitors combine it with
Dahican Beach

and Mount Hamiguitan in a 2-day or 3-day trip. From central Mati the pier is under 20 minutes away by habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) or tricycle, so staying in town makes an early boat departure easy. Island trips depend heavily on weather and tides, so keep one spare day in your plan in case a trip is canceled.

The island is about 156 hectares, with white sand and clear water. It has cottages, simple tables and toilets, and a caretaker collects the island fee. Shade is limited, so bring a hat and sunscreen. On a day trip it is often the first stop, so early in the day you can walk a quiet beach with few other visitors.
This is considered the best swimming stop on the island tour, good for splashing around and snorkeling. Whether you can land depends on the tide and weather.

These small islets appear as white sandbars at low tide and disappear at high tide. The surrounding reef can be exposed at low tide, so snorkeling is safer close to high tide. Take care not to stand on the coral. The time the sandbar appears depends on that day's tide table, so ask your lodging or boatman for the low and high tide times.

Around the small lighthouse at the southeastern tip of Pujada Island you can take in the bay entrance and the Pacific at a glance. As the boat passes through one of the two channels, you will notice the color of the sea change abruptly.

The roughly 850 hectares of mangroves and seagrass beds inside the bay are the foundation of the ecosystem. You can see mangroves up close on the boardwalk at Guanguan Mangrove Park. Do not step on coral or seagrass, and do not take shells or sand.

Pujada Island is recommended as a freediving spot in Mati. Ordinary visitors can enjoy it fully with just a mask and a life jacket for snorkeling. Be sure to check before departure whether equipment and life jackets are included in the boat fee.

The Pujada Bay Festival is held in mid-June, and Mati and the pier get busy. Boats and rooms fill up quickly during the festival, so book early. Check the City of Mati's announcements for exact dates.

items.title: Day island tour
items.subtitle: Hop between three islands from the Tamisan pier

children.text: From central Mati, take a habal-habal or tricycle to the Batiano pier (Pier One) in Barangay Tamisan. It usually takes
15–20 minutes
Hire a boat and confirm that life jackets and snorkeling gear are provided. Waves get rougher in the afternoon, so leave as early as you can.
Land first on Pujada Island. Pay the island fee, claim a cottage for your things, walk the beach and enjoy the view toward the lighthouse.
Head to Oak Island and, if the tide allows, take photos on the sandbar and snorkel.
Have lunch and swim at Waniban Island. There are no shops there, so bring a packed lunch.
Return to the pier before the wind picks up. The usual tour wraps up around 4:30 PM.

The boat fee is per boat, not per person, so the more people in your group, the less each pays. Depending on tide, weather and protected-area rules, which islands you can visit may change. Adjust the pace to your group and the waves, and agree on the return time with the boatman in advance.
Take a Mati-bound bus from the Ecoland terminal in Davao. Buses start running in the early morning, and the trip takes about 3–4 hours.
Check in in central Mati and visit Guanguan Mangrove Park and the town. Watching the sunset at Dahican Beach is also a good idea.
Get up early and do the day island tour above. In the afternoon, return to Davao by bus or van.
Check the last departure to Davao at the Mati bus terminal in advance.
Direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Francisco Bangoy International Airport (DVO) in Davao take about
1 hour 40 minutes to 2 hours 10 minutes
(varies by flight). Several airlines fly daily.
Mati has no scheduled flights for ordinary travelers, so the standard route is to fly to Davao City and continue by road.
Flight schedules, fares and flight times differ by flight and change often, so check with the airline when you book.
Air-conditioned buses to Mati from the Ecoland bus terminal start at about
and take
3–4 hours
. They begin running in the early morning.
Vans leaving from in front of Gaisano Mall start at about
and are faster, at
2.5–3 hours
A rental car or a car with a driver lets you set your own schedule and is a good value for larger groups.

Bus fares differ by company and season; one air-conditioned bus was reported at around ₱392 and about 4 hours (a fuel surcharge may apply). Bus and van fares and schedules vary, so check at the terminal.
From the Mati terminal to the Tamisan pier takes about
15–20 minutes
by habal-habal or tricycle, costing about
(ask whether a return wait is included before you negotiate).
The pier is the Batiano pier (Pier One) in Tamisan, not on the Dahican Beach side. From Dahican, take a tricycle to the pier.

The calmest period is described as March through early May, when fewer island trips are canceled and the water is clearer. Rain is heaviest from May to July and in November, so leave some slack in your plans then.
In any season, it is best to take the boat in the morning. Waves grow in the afternoon, and the Oak Island side in particular gets rough.

Lodging is centered on Mati town and the resorts along Dahican Beach. Dahican has several surf resorts and beachfront cottages, and there are beach resorts near the pier around Tamisan. To catch an early boat, staying around Tamisan or in town is more convenient. Check booking sites for current prices and whether a property is operating.

There are almost no shops on the islands, so buy packed lunches, fruit and water at the Mati market or your lodging. Some resorts will prepare a lunch for your boat tour if you ask. Always take your trash back with you.

Mati town has local eateries and a market where you can try grilled fish and seafood, coconut and tropical fruit at low prices. Buying lunch ingredients and water the evening before makes the early start much easier. Use the exchange shops and ATMs in town during the day, and bring plenty of small bills before heading to the islands.
Many travelers say boarding at the Batiano pier in Tamisan is closer and cheaper. Booking through a resort is convenient but can cost more.
Before departure, confirm whether the boat price is per boat, whether snorkeling gear and life jackets are included, and whether the island fee is extra.
Pay the island fee in cash. There are no ATMs on the islands, so bring enough cash.
The reef around Oak Island is exposed at low tide, so plan snorkeling close to high tide.
To stay ahead of the afternoon waves, do the farthest island first in the morning.
Pack a dry bag, reef shoes, a hat, sunscreen, water and snacks. Shade is scarce.
Do not step on coral or seagrass, feed the fish, or take shells or sand. Follow the protected-area rules.
Book your boat and room early around the Pujada Bay Festival in mid-June.
The boatman knows the day's waves and tides better than anyone. Tell him which island you would like to visit, but follow his lead if he suggests changing the route for safety.
Mobile signal can be weak inside the bay and on the islands, so agree on how to stay in touch and a meeting time beforehand.

Boats do not sail when weather advisories are issued or the sea is rough. Check on the morning of your trip at the pier and in the City of Mati's announcements, and make sure everyone on board wears a life jacket.
The island fee and boat rates differ between sources, so confirm them locally.
Depending on the tide, some islands such as Oak may not be landable, or the sandbar may disappear.
There are no shops or medical facilities on the islands, so bring basic medicine and drinking water.
Waves grow in the afternoon, so avoid a late start.
Under protected-area rules, collecting coral, feeding fish and removing sand or shells are prohibited. Rules can change, so check the latest announcements.
